case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbour Bay Poultry (HBP) is a private limited company in the food processing sector, converting fresh chicken into frozen ready-to-cook meals sold through national supermarket chains. Founded in 2012 by Jernej Munoz, the business employs a workforce of 42. It operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. HBP plans to invest $720,000 in a new frozen-line grading and packaging plant with contactless automation, financed by a ten-year bank loan and retained profit. It has fixed costs of $620,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.50 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and currently produces 180,000 units a year. HBP faces a worsening defect rate record on sealing and rising quality complaint levels from retail buyers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2026: The frozen meal line has grown to 180,000 units produced a year, up from 155,000 a year ago. Defect rate on sealing is now 3.9%, down from 5.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 27 per month. Average delivery time to processors is 1.9 days. A survey of 320 processors found that 62% would pay a $2.10 premium per meal for eco-packaging, and 48% check shelf life before buying. Off-the-job training at the regional college costs $800 per employee; 12 of the 42 staff need recertification of the new freezing equipment.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harbour Bay Poultry as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The national minimum wage rises by 7.5% from $13.50 to $14.51 per hour from May 2026, raising total wage bills for HBP's 42 employees. (2) Agricultural nitrogen and fuel input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while food-price inflation is running at 6.9%. (3) Consumer spending on ready-to-cook frozen meals fell 2.1% while spending on fresh chilled meals grew 4.7% in the same period.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for HBP of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs HBP nothing in repayments or interest on the $720,000 expansion, so every dollar not paid as loan interest can absorb the 6.9% rise in agricultural input costs, keeping the $16.50 meals affordable to supermarket buyers and defending the $4.00 contribution ($16.50 − $12.50) during the $620,000 plant build. It also avoids the collateral and default risk attached to the ten-year bank loan, so the whole frozen-line grading and packaging plant is not at risk of repossession.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership with the management team, so no lender can impose conditions on how HBP runs the freezing automation or sets prices; HBP keeps full flexibility to reinvest surplus into further capacity or quality improvements once the plant stabilises.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to HBP's expansion, contribution and ownership.

questions.question_text: Consider a national frozen-meals marketing campaign, local TV sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should HBP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
1. National frozen-meals marketing campaign: a national TV campaign reaches millions of buyers quickly, but airtime and production costs are extremely high, so much of the spend would be wasted on viewers outside HBP's supermarket footprint or buyers of unfrozen meals.

2. Local TV sponsorship: cheaper than national TV, suits time-sensitive launch messages near supermarkets, but local reach alone cannot generate the volume needed to justify the 180,000-unit output plan across national supermarket chains.

3. Social media influencer marketing: food and family lifestyle influencers show the frozen meals being cooked, sliced and delivered, targeting the retail buyers described in appendix 1 who pay up to $16.50 per meal; cost per reached shopper is low and results are measurable in pre-orders.

Recommendation: HBP should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets retail buyers described in the appendix, fits the $720,000 plant better than national TV, and supports the launch; national TV is rejected as too costly for the $4.00 contribution margins, and local TV as too narrow for national supermarket listings; HBP should add modest in-store tasting sessions with supermarkets as a support to the influencer campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HBP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HBP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why national TV and local TV are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for HBP of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its kitchen and freezing teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HBP's 42 staff a genuine voice in rota planning, oven schedules and equipment maintenance, which satisfies their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help decide shift patterns and press sealing are more likely to attend reliably, directly attacking the rising quality complaint levels from retail buyers.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions surfaces practical ideas from the people who handle frozen meals daily, improving sealing quality and pushing the 3.9% defect rate down further. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, saving HBP's $800 per employee off-the-job recertification cost while protecting the 180,000-unit output plan during the plant build.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to HBP's attendance, quality and output.

questions.question_text: HBP must upskill 12 production staff on the new freezing equipment before the new plant opens. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should HBP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training on HBP's own freezing equipment is directly relevant, costs nothing in course fees and keeps the 12 staff productive during the run-up to the plant opening, protecting the 180,000-unit output plan. Drawbacks are that trainers are production staff whose own work suffers, and bad habits can be passed on informally.

Off-the-job training: The $800 per employee course at the regional college gives structured, certified hygiene training.

Decision: HBP should choose on-the-job training for the 12 staff, with short college sessions for lead operators added after launch. On-the-job training is cheapest and machine-specific while capacity is needed; the $800 college course is used later for broader skills. HBP will still need the $800 per employee recertification to satisfy auditors — off-the-job training is rejected because removing 12 staff from the line during the launch period hurts output.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HBP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the training methods in the context of HBP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HBP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $620,000 ÷ ($16.50 − $12.50) = $620,000 ÷ $4.00 = 155,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 155,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.50 − $12.50 = $4.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HBP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Margin of safety: HBP produces 180,000 units against a break-even of 155,000, leaving about 25,000 units of buffer before profit turns negative.
2. Pricing: at $16.50 each, the $4.00 contribution covers the $620,000 fixed costs after 155,000 units, so discount modelling must keep the contribution above that level.
3. Loan repayments: the $4.00 contribution tells managers how many units the $720,000 expansion needs before the bank loan is serviced from profits.
4. Cost benchmarking: average total cost is about $15.94 per unit against the $620,000 fixed-cost base, helping benchmark the warehouse waste behind the rising complaint levels.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HBP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HBP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.49 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.47 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.91 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $58,000 inventories + $42,000 receivables + $31,000 cash = $131,000; excluding inventories leaves $73,000 against $88,000. 2025 current assets = $54,000 + $47,000 + $39,000 = $140,000; excluding inventories leaves $86,000 against $95,000.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved slightly. The current ratio is similar, while current liabilities rose from $88,000 to $95,000 with assets growing, so HBP covers short-term obligations with a reasonable margin. The acid test improved from 0.83 to 0.91, so HBP no longer relies on selling stock to meet short-term debts; the margin of safety for retail buyers grew. Trade receivables rose from $42,000 to $47,000, and inventories fell, so cash should be monitored while the $620,000 plant is built.

Conclusion: HBP's financial position has improved, as shown by the stronger acid test ratio (0.83 to 0.91).

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether HBP's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HBP of introducing eco-packaging with extended shelf life for its frozen ready-to-cook meals.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-packaging matches the preferences of the 62% of 320 surveyed processors who would pay a $2.10 premium per meal for it, allowing HBP to charge a premium that protects the $16.50 selling price and the $4.00 contribution ($16.50 − $12.50) during the $620,000 plant build. It also strengthens HBP's brand image with the 48% of buyers who check shelf life, helping win or retain supermarket listings.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials typically cost more than conventional plastic, which would increase HBP's $12.50 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $2.10 premium is accepted on the whole range. Any failure in eco-materials (for example, shorter shelf life for frozen meals) would raise the current 3.9% defect rate and increase waste before the plant stabilises.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HBP's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 7.5% minimum wage rise to $14.51 per hour, the 14.2% agricultural-input cost inflation and the 2.1% fall in ready-to-cook frozen-meal consumer spending will affect HBP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
The 7.5% minimum wage rise to $14.51 per hour: with a workforce of 42, most of which is hourly-paid, this feeds directly into HBP's wage bill. The insert does not give hours worked, so the honest judgement is against productivity data: 180,000 units ÷ 42 staff = about 4,286 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds at that level or output grows.

The 14.2% agricultural-input inflation: this compounds on every one of HBP's 180,000 units and directly erodes the $4.00 contribution ($16.50 − $12.50). If the entire $12.50 variable cost rose 14.2%, that would be $1.78 per unit, and at the 180,000 units HBP produces a year that is about $320,000 of extra cost; a realistic share of ingredient costs rose, so the true impact lies between $45,000 and $60,000 of extra cost per year. HBP can recover part of it through the $2.10 eco-packaging premium and supermarket price negotiations, both given in appendix 1.

The 2.1% fall in frozen-meal consumer spending: weak demand softens HBP's 180,000-unit plan, though spending on fresh chilled meals grew 4.7%, so the fall is partially offset by the rising fresh-meal segment.

Conclusion: the 14.2% input-cost inflation will have the greatest impact on HBP, because it is charged on every unit of the 180,000-unit output and directly erodes the $4.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 expansion. HBP should negotiate ingredient prices or lock in supply contracts now and lean on the $2.10 premium to claw back margin.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HBP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HBP's costs or demand in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
